title: AudioSphere: Towards Self-Supervised Spatial Audio Representation Models
claim: A masked autoencoder pretrained on multichannel spatial audio yields a frozen encoder that serves both frame-level and clip-level downstream tasks.
layout: 2 stacked panels (A pretraining, B inference), left-to-right flow, branching outputs
description: Two horizontal rows, labeled A and B. Panel A (pre-training) flows left to right. Colored Ambisonics waveforms (W, Y, Z, X) become stacked mel spectrograms and intensity-vector maps. These are concatenated and masked into a checkerboard of gray patches. The data then goes through a teal Encoder, a column of orange tokens with gray masked slots, a Decoder, and a reconstructed sound-field stack. Panel B (inference) starts with icons of diverse microphone arrays. 'Ambisonics Signal Matching' converts their signals into the same spectrogram and intensity-vector stacks, which are concatenated and passed through the Encoder. The encoder outputs a column of frame tokens. A dashed path goes to a Mean Pooling box and a list of clip-level tasks. A second dashed path, labeled Frame Level, goes to a sphere localization plot and an event timeline for SELD. Large labels sit above each stage, and the heat-map textures draw the eye first.
caption: (A) Pre-Training: We employ the Masked Autoencoder (MAE) approach to learn spatial audio representations. Ambisonics recordings are converted into mel spectrograms and Intensity Vectors, concatenated, and masked. The Encoder processes unmasked patches and the Decoder reconstructs the original full sound field. (B) Inference: The pre-trained Encoder can be flexibly applied to diverse microphone arrays. Diverse input signals are standardized via Ambisonics Signal Matching and passed through the Encoder to extract frame-level and scene-level Ambisonics embeddings.
abstract: Recent audio embedding models learn representations that transfer across clip- and frame-level tasks, yet they operate almost exclusively on single-channel signals and are blind to spatial structure. Spatial audio models capture that structure but rely on clip-level supervision or contrastive objectives, yielding embeddings unsuitable for frame-level tasks like sound event detection and localization (SELD). We argue this dichotomy is not fundamental: patch-level spatial self-supervision can jointly learn acoustic and spatial features at both temporal granularities. We introduce AudioSphere, a multi-channel masked autoencoder trained on Ambisonics recordings that reconstructs both spectral content and directional cues via a joint spatiotemporal masking strategy that masks both time-frequency patches and intensity vectors. AudioSphere supports frame-level predictions while producing strong clip-level representations via aggregation. Alongside the model, we release RealSELD, a standardized benchmark for evaluating frozen backbones on real-world multi-channel SELD. AudioSphere enables, for the first time, SELD with a frozen self-supervised backbone, while matching or exceeding prior self-supervised audio embedding models on clip-level classification tasks spanning environmental sound, speech, and music, and on frame-level sound event detection. All code and data are available at https://github.com/labhamlet/AudioSphere and https://huggingface.co/labhamlet.
